title: The Respiratory System
description: Week 11: the upper and lower airways, the lungs and pleura, the breathing muscles and their nerves, ventilation, gas exchange, and oxygen transport, pulmonary function tests, the respiratory history and lung exam, common respiratory disorders, and influenza with infection control.

outbreak.intro: A nurse at a long-term care facility is caring for an 81-year-old resident during an outbreak of influenza A on the unit.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html:
Nurses' Notes

Day 1, 0900: Rapid influenza test positive for influenza A. Reports muscle aches, a sore throat, and a headache. Dry cough. Moved to a private room on droplet precautions. Provider notified; antiviral medication prescribed.

Day 4, 0800: Resident is newly confused about the day and place, and is coughing up thick, rust-colored sputum. Reports a sharp pain in the right lower chest when breathing in. Ate 25% of breakfast. Respirations labored. Right lower posterior chest: dull to percussion, increased tactile fremitus, bronchial breath sounds and crackles. Left lung: vesicular breath sounds. Lips pink.

questions.stem: A client with a head cold says, “My voice sounds muffled and flat, and my cheeks and forehead ache.” Which structures should the nurse suspect are swollen?
options: The paranasal sinuses, which help give the voice its resonance
The vocal folds of the larynx, which vibrate to make the sound of the voice
The turbinates, which make the air swirl so that it's warmed and filtered
The epiglottis, which closes over the larynx during swallowing
questions.rationale:
The paranasal sinuses (frontal, maxillary, ethmoid, and sphenoid) help give the voice its resonance and condition the air. Swollen, blocked sinuses make the voice sound muffled and flat, and aching cheeks and forehead point to the maxillary and frontal sinuses.

The vocal folds are the tempting choice, since they make the voice, but swollen vocal folds make a voice hoarse, not muffled, and wouldn't explain the facial pain. The turbinates warm, moisten, and filter air, and the epiglottis protects the airway during swallowing.

Takeaway: Sinuses: resonance of the voice. Larynx (vocal folds): the sound itself, so hoarseness.

questions.stem: During an oral exam, a nurse sees swollen tonsils at the back of the mouth, just behind the arch at the back of the oral cavity. Which part of the pharynx is the nurse looking at?
options: The nasopharynx, behind the nasal cavity and above the palate
The hypopharynx, which leads into both the larynx and the esophagus
The oropharynx, between the palate and the hyoid bone
The larynx, where the vocal folds form the glottic opening
questions.rationale:
The oropharynx lies between the palate and the hyoid bone, and is separated from the mouth by the tonsillar arch, so tonsils seen at the back of the mouth are in the oropharynx.

The nasopharynx is the tempting choice, since it holds lymphoid tissue too (the adenoids), but it sits above the palate, behind the nose, out of sight in an oral exam. The hypopharynx begins below the hyoid bone, and the larynx isn't part of the pharynx.

Takeaway: Nasopharynx (behind the nose, above the palate), oropharynx (behind the mouth, to the hyoid), hypopharynx (below the hyoid, into the larynx and esophagus).

questions.stem: A client recovering from a stroke coughs and sputters whenever drinking thin liquids. Which structure should the nurse suspect isn't sealing off the airway in time during swallowing?
options: The soft palate, which rises to close off the nasal cavity
The thyroid cartilage, the largest cartilage at the front of the neck
The cricoid cartilage, the ring at the bottom of the larynx
The epiglottis, which folds down over the opening of the larynx
questions.rationale:
During swallowing, the epiglottis folds down over the opening of the larynx (the glottis), so liquid goes into the esophagus instead of the airway. When it closes late, liquid slips into the larynx and triggers coughing.

The soft palate is the tempting choice, since it also closes during swallowing, but it seals off the nasal cavity, not the airway to the lungs. The thyroid and cricoid cartilages form the framework of the larynx; they don't close over it.

Takeaway: Swallowing: the soft palate closes the nose, and the epiglottis covers the larynx.

questions.stem: A few minutes after a bee sting, a client develops a loud, high-pitched sound on every breath in, which the nurse can hear without a stethoscope. Click the structure where the airway is most likely narrowed.
questions.alt: Front view of the airways and lungs, with the client's right on the viewer's left, marked R and L: the larynx at the top, the trachea below it dividing into two main bronchi, a right lung divided by two fissure lines into three parts and a left lung divided by one fissure line into two parts, all the same color, and a curved band of muscle under both lungs.
questions.rationale:
A loud, high-pitched sound on inspiration is stridor, a sign of upper airway obstruction. Heard on breathing in, it means the narrowing is above the chest, as in swelling of the larynx during an allergic reaction. It's an emergency: the airway can close.

The bronchi are the tempting choice, since narrowed bronchi make high-pitched sounds too, but those are wheezes, from the lower airways, usually heard on breathing out.

Takeaway: Stridor = upper airway obstruction (on breathing in: above the chest, like the larynx). Wheezes = lower airways.

questions.stem: An adult inhales a piece of peanut while laughing, and it passes through the larynx and trachea. Click the airway where it most likely lodges.
questions.alt: Front view of the airways and lungs, with the client's right on the viewer's left, marked R and L: the larynx at the top, the trachea below it dividing into two main bronchi, a right lung divided by two fissure lines into three parts and a left lung divided by one fissure line into two parts, all the same color, and a curved band of muscle under both lungs.
questions.rationale:
The right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical than the left, almost a straight line down from the trachea, so inhaled objects and aspirated material most often go to the right.

The left main bronchus is the tempting choice, since it's the longer passage, but it leaves the trachea at a sharper angle, so objects tend to bypass it.

Takeaway: Right main bronchus: wider, shorter, more vertical, so more prone to aspiration.

questions.stem: A client who was sitting upright vomited and aspirated some of it. Three days later, the nurse hears crackles over one lobe. Click the lobe most likely affected.
questions.alt: Front view of the airways and lungs, with the client's right on the viewer's left, marked R and L: the larynx at the top, the trachea below it dividing into two main bronchi, a right lung divided by two fissure lines into three parts and a left lung divided by one fissure line into two parts, all the same color, and a curved band of muscle under both lungs.
questions.rationale:
Aspirated material follows gravity and the straightest path. Upright, it runs down the wider, more vertical right main bronchus to the lowest part of the right lung, the right lower lobe.

The right middle lobe is the tempting choice, since it's on the right side too, but its bronchus branches off toward the front, while the material falls straight down. The upper lobes are more often involved when a client aspirates lying down.

Takeaway: Aspiration while upright: the right lower lobe (gravity plus the vertical right bronchus).

questions.stem: A nurse auscultates a client's back and hears clear breath sounds over every area. A chest x-ray, however, shows pneumonia in the one lobe that can be heard only from the front and the right side of the chest. Click that lobe.
questions.alt: Front view of the airways and lungs, with the client's right on the viewer's left, marked R and L: the larynx at the top, the trachea below it dividing into two main bronchi, a right lung divided by two fissure lines into three parts and a left lung divided by one fissure line into two parts, all the same color, and a curved band of muscle under both lungs.
questions.rationale:
The right middle lobe, between the horizontal and oblique fissures, lies toward the front of the right chest. It's heard from the front and the right side, not from the back, which is why a back-only assessment missed it.

The right lower lobe is the tempting choice, since it's also on the right, but most of it lies toward the back: pneumonia there would have changed the sounds on the client's back.

Takeaway: A complete lung exam covers the front and sides too: the right middle lobe can't be heard from the back.

questions.stem: A nurse is comparing the two lungs. For each feature, specify the lung it describes.
rows: Has three lobes
Has a cardiac notch, where the heart sits
Its main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical
Has only one fissure, the oblique fissure
Is covered by visceral pleura
questions.rationale:
The right lung has three lobes (upper, middle, lower), separated by the horizontal and oblique fissures, and its main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical. The left lung has two lobes, separated only by the oblique fissure, and a cardiac notch that makes room for the heart. Both lungs are covered by visceral pleura; the parietal pleura lines the chest wall.

The bronchus is the row most often missed: the right one is the more vertical, which is why aspiration goes right.

Takeaway: Right: 3 lobes, 2 fissures, the vertical bronchus. Left: 2 lobes, 1 fissure, the cardiac notch.

questions.stem: A client's chest x-ray shows fluid collecting between the visceral and parietal pleura at the base of the left lung. Which findings should the nurse expect over that area?
options: Dull percussion, and decreased tactile fremitus
Dull percussion, and increased tactile fremitus with crackles
Hyperresonant percussion, and decreased tactile fremitus
Resonant percussion, and soft, low-pitched vesicular breath sounds
questions.rationale:
Fluid in the pleural space (a pleural effusion) sounds dull when percussed, and it separates the lung from the chest wall, which damps the vibrations of the voice: tactile fremitus decreases.

Dull percussion with increased fremitus is the tempting choice, since the dullness is right, but fremitus increases only when the lung tissue itself is denser, as in pneumonia. Hyperresonance means air in the pleural space (a pneumothorax), and resonance with vesicular sounds is normal.

Takeaway: Fremitus goes up with denser lung tissue (consolidation), and down when something separates the lung from the chest wall (fluid or air).

questions.stem: Nerve damage at the C3 to C5 level has paralyzed a client's diaphragm. Which finding should the nurse expect?
options: Breathing that stays normal at rest, since the intercostal muscles do most of the work
Rapid, shallow breathing, with the neck muscles tightening on each breath
Slow, deep breathing, since each breath takes longer to draw in
Labored breathing out, while breathing in stays easy
questions.rationale:
The diaphragm, supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5), is the main muscle of inspiration. Without it, breaths are shallow, the rate rises to make up for it, and the accessory muscles of the neck (the sternocleidomastoid and scalenes) work on every breath.

“The intercostals do most of the work” is the tempting choice, since they do help, but they work mainly during exercise and distress; at rest the diaphragm does most of the work. Breathing in is what's impaired, not breathing out.

Takeaway: C3, C4, and C5 keep the diaphragm alive: the phrenic nerve. Without it, the accessory muscles take over.

questions.stem: During an assessment, a client sits leaning forward with both hands on the knees, and the muscles of the neck tighten with each breath. How should the nurse interpret these findings?
options: The client is working hard to breathe, and is using the accessory muscles
The client is in a position of comfort that doesn't point to a breathing problem
The neck muscles are tense from coughing, not from the work of breathing
The client is guarding against back pain, so the nurse should assess the spine
questions.rationale:
Leaning forward with the hands on the knees is the tripod position, which clients in respiratory distress take, and neck muscles that tighten with each breath are accessory muscles (the sternocleidomastoid and scalenes) helping to breathe. Together, they show a high work of breathing.

Tense from coughing is the tempting choice, since coughing does use these muscles, but tightening with every breath, while leaning forward, is accessory muscle use. A position of comfort or back pain doesn't explain the neck muscles.

Takeaway: Tripod position plus accessory muscles = working hard to breathe.

questions.stem: Complete the following sentence about breathing in.
questions.text: During inspiration, the diaphragm {{0}} and moves {{1}}, which {{2}} the volume of the chest, so air flows into the lungs.

options: relaxes
contracts
downward
upward
decreases
increases

questions.rationale:
The diaphragm is the main muscle of inspiration and forms the floor of the chest. When it contracts, it flattens and moves downward, which increases the volume of the chest, and air flows in. When it relaxes, it rises again, and air flows out.

The trap is picturing the diaphragm pushing up to breathe in; it's the other way around.

Takeaway: Breathing in: the diaphragm contracts and moves down, and the chest gets bigger.

questions.stem: A client with emphysema breathes out slowly through pursed lips. What does this breathing pattern do for the client?
options: It pulls more oxygen into the lungs with each breath in
It strengthens the diaphragm so that it can push the air out
It narrows the airways to keep dust out of the alveoli
It keeps the airways open longer, so trapped air can leave
questions.rationale:
In emphysema, the alveoli lose their elasticity, so air gets trapped and the small airways collapse when the client breathes out. Breathing out slowly through pursed lips keeps a little pressure in the airways, holding them open longer so more of the trapped air leaves.

Pulling in more oxygen is the tempting choice, since the client is short of breath, but pursed lips act on breathing out. They don't strengthen the diaphragm or filter dust.

Takeaway: Emphysema traps air; pursed-lip breathing helps get it out.

questions.stem: A client with severe anemia (hemoglobin 7 g/dL) has an oxygen saturation of 98% but feels short of breath and tired. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: A saturation of 98% means the tissues are getting enough oxygen, so the symptoms have another cause
Most oxygen travels dissolved in the plasma, so a low hemoglobin has little effect on oxygen delivery
The saturation shows how full the hemoglobin is, but with so little hemoglobin, the blood carries less oxygen
A pulse oximeter can't read a hemoglobin this low, so the 98% is probably wrong
questions.rationale:
Oxygen content depends mostly on hemoglobin: CaO₂ = 1.34 × Hgb × (SaO₂ ÷ 100) + 0.003 × PaO₂. Saturation is only the percentage of hemoglobin carrying oxygen. With little hemoglobin, a full 98% still adds up to much less oxygen for the tissues.

“98% means enough oxygen” is the tempting choice, since saturation is the number nurses watch most, but it says nothing about how much hemoglobin there is. Dissolved oxygen (0.003 × PaO₂) is only a tiny part of the total, and a normal saturation reading isn't an error.

Takeaway: Oxygen content = mostly hemoglobin × saturation. A normal SpO₂ can hide low oxygen delivery in anemia.

questions.stem: A newborn born at 28 weeks has alveoli that collapse at the end of each breath. Which cells are most likely not making enough of their secretion yet?
options: Type I pneumocytes, which line the alveoli for gas exchange
Type II pneumocytes, which secrete surfactant
Alveolar macrophages, which defend against pathogens and irritants
Ciliated cells of the trachea, which move mucus toward the throat
questions.rationale:
Type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant, which lowers the surface tension inside the alveoli so they don't collapse at the end of each breath. In a very premature newborn, these cells don't make enough yet.

Type I pneumocytes are the tempting choice, since they line the alveoli, but they're the thin cells where gas exchange happens; they don't make surfactant. Macrophages (dust cells) defend the alveoli, and ciliated cells clear mucus from the airways.

Takeaway: Type I: gas exchange. Type II: surfactant, which keeps the alveoli open.

questions.stem: A client's respiratory rate is 18/min, and the chest rises fully and evenly with each breath, but the oxygen saturation keeps falling as fluid builds up in the alveoli. Which process is most impaired?
options: Ventilation, the movement of air into and out of the alveoli
The nerves' control of the breathing muscles
Perfusion, the flow of blood through the pulmonary arteries
Gas exchange between the alveoli and the blood (respiration)
questions.rationale:
Ventilation is the movement of air in and out, and here it's working: a normal rate and full, even chest rise. Respiration, the exchange of gases by diffusion between the alveoli and the capillary blood, is what's failing: fluid in the alveoli thickens the barrier oxygen must cross.

Ventilation is the tempting choice, since the client has a lung problem and a falling saturation, but air is still moving. Nothing points to the nerves or to blocked blood flow.

Takeaway: Ventilation moves air; respiration exchanges gases. A client can ventilate well and still not oxygenate.

questions.stem: A blood clot blocks blood flow to part of a client's lung (a pulmonary embolism), but air still moves in and out of those alveoli. Which describes the affected area?
options: Ventilated but not perfused, so no gas exchange happens there
Perfused but not ventilated, so blood passes through without picking up oxygen
Neither ventilated nor perfused, because the alveoli have collapsed
Ventilated and perfused normally, since the clot is in a blood vessel
questions.rationale:
Gas exchange needs both ventilation (air reaching the alveoli) and perfusion (blood reaching their capillaries). A clot blocks the blood, so the area is ventilated but not perfused: air comes and goes without any exchange, a ventilation-perfusion mismatch.

Perfused but not ventilated is the tempting choice, since it's the other common mismatch, but that's the pattern of blocked or fluid-filled alveoli, as in pneumonia. Here the air moves; the blood doesn't.

Takeaway: Clot: air without blood. Pneumonia or a mucus plug: blood without air. Either way, oxygenation suffers.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing what determines how much oxygen the blood carries. For each change, specify its effect on the blood's oxygen content.
rows: Hemoglobin falls from 14 to 8 g/dL, with the oxygen saturation still 98%
Oxygen saturation falls from 98% to 80%, with a normal hemoglobin
Hemoglobin rises from 9 to 14 g/dL after a blood transfusion
PaO₂ rises from 95 to 110 mm Hg, with the saturation already 99%
Supplemental oxygen raises the saturation from 84% to 95%
questions.rationale:
Oxygen content (CaO₂ = 1.34 × Hgb × SaO₂ + 0.003 × PaO₂) depends mostly on hemoglobin and saturation. A falling hemoglobin or saturation lowers it, and a rising one (after a transfusion, or with oxygen for a low saturation) raises it.

The PaO₂ row is the trap: a higher PaO₂ looks like more oxygen, but when the hemoglobin is already almost fully saturated, the only gain is dissolved oxygen, which is multiplied by just 0.003, so the content barely changes.

Takeaway: To raise oxygen content: more hemoglobin, or a higher saturation. PaO₂ alone adds little once hemoglobin is full.

questions.stem: A client with asthma uses an inhaler that acts like the sympathetic nervous system on the airways. Which effect should the nurse expect?
options: The airways narrow, and the glands make more mucus
The diaphragm contracts harder, so each breath is deeper
The airways widen, and the wheezing eases
The heart rate slows, so the client feels calmer
questions.rationale:
The lungs' nerves come from the pulmonary plexus. Sympathetic stimulation causes bronchodilation (and less gland secretion), so an inhaler that acts like it widens the airways and eases wheezing.

Narrowed airways and more mucus is the tempting choice, since it's the textbook pairing, but it's the effect of the parasympathetic (vagus) nerves. The phrenic nerve, not the sympathetic system, drives the diaphragm, and sympathetic effects speed the heart rather than slow it.

Takeaway: Airways: sympathetic = bronchodilation; parasympathetic (vagus) = bronchoconstriction and more secretions.

questions.stem: A client who has asthma is prescribed propranolol, a beta blocker, for high blood pressure. What should the nurse do?
options: Give the first dose, and teach the client to keep the rescue inhaler close by
Check with the prescriber, since beta blockers can narrow the airways
Give it with food, since beta blockers irritate the stomach and set off coughing
Hold the client's asthma inhaler, and ask the prescriber whether it can still be used
questions.rationale:
Beta blockers (and NSAIDs) can cause bronchoconstriction, which in a client with asthma can set off an attack. The nurse checks with the prescriber before giving it.

Giving it with the rescue inhaler close by is the tempting choice, since it sounds like a safe compromise, but it plans for an attack instead of preventing one. Food has nothing to do with the problem, and holding the client's asthma inhaler would make it worse; the question for the prescriber is about the beta blocker.

Takeaway: Drug history for breathing problems: beta blockers and NSAIDs (bronchoconstriction), ACE inhibitors (dry cough), estrogen (clots).

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing lung volumes and capacities. Complete the following sentences.
questions.text: The {{0}} is the air left in the lungs after a maximal breath out, which spirometry can't measure. Adding it to the vital capacity gives the {{1}}. The air breathed in and out in a normal breath is the {{2}}.
questions.rationale:
The residual volume stays in the lungs even after a maximal exhalation, so spirometry, which measures air moved, can't measure it. Vital capacity + residual volume = total lung capacity, the air in the lungs after a maximal breath in. A normal breath is the tidal volume.

The functional residual capacity is the tempting token for the first blank, but it's the air left after a normal breath out (the expiratory reserve volume plus the residual volume).

Takeaway: Residual volume: left after a maximal exhale, can't be measured by spirometry. TLC = VC + RV.

questions.stem: A client's spirometry shows an inspiratory reserve volume of {irv} mL, a tidal volume of {tv} mL, and an expiratory reserve volume of {erv} mL. The residual volume, measured another way, is {rv} mL. What vital capacity should the nurse record?
questions.rationale:
Vital capacity is the most air the client can breathe out after a maximal breath in: the inspiratory reserve volume + the tidal volume + the expiratory reserve volume = {irv} + {tv} + {erv} = {answer} mL.

The residual volume is the trap: it stays in the lungs, so it isn't part of the vital capacity. Adding it ({=irv + tv + erv + rv} mL) gives the total lung capacity instead.

Takeaway: Vital capacity = IRV + TV + ERV. Total lung capacity = vital capacity + residual volume.

questions.stem: A client's spirometry shows a forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) of {fev1} L and a forced vital capacity (FVC) of {fvc} L. What FEV1/FVC ratio, as a percentage, should the nurse record?
questions.rationale:
FEV1/FVC = {fev1} L ÷ {fvc} L × 100 = {=round(fev1 / fvc * 100, 2)}%, which rounds to {answer}%.

Reading it: in obstructive disease (asthma, COPD), air can't get out quickly, so the FEV1 falls much more than the FVC and the ratio drops well below normal. In restrictive disease, both fall, so the ratio stays normal or rises. The usual mistake is dividing the other way ({=round(fvc / fev1 * 100)}%).

Takeaway: FEV1/FVC = FEV1 ÷ FVC × 100. A ratio well below normal points to obstruction.

questions.stem: A client's spirometry shows a low forced vital capacity and a low FEV1, with an FEV1/FVC ratio higher than normal. Which condition fits this pattern?
options: Asthma, with airways that narrow and swell in attacks
Emphysema, with alveoli that lose their elasticity
Pulmonary fibrosis, with scarred, stiffened lung tissue
Chronic bronchitis, with inflamed, mucus-filled airways
questions.rationale:
This is a restrictive pattern: the lungs can't expand fully, so the FVC falls even more than the FEV1, and the ratio stays normal or rises. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, scarring that stiffens the lung tissue, is a restrictive disease.

Asthma is the tempting choice, since its FEV1 is low too, but asthma, emphysema, and chronic bronchitis are obstructive: air can't get out, so the FEV1/FVC ratio drops sharply.

Takeaway: Obstructive: ratio down (air can't get out). Restrictive: ratio normal or up (the lungs can't fill).

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing a client for a methacholine challenge test to check for asthma. Which item should the nurse have ready at the bedside before the test starts?
options: An incentive spirometer, for deep breathing after the test
A rapid-acting bronchodilator, such as albuterol
An epinephrine auto-injector, for a possible allergic reaction
A sterile cup, for a sputum specimen during the test
questions.rationale:
A methacholine challenge (bronchoprovocation) deliberately narrows the airways to see how reactive they are, so severe bronchospasm can happen. A rapid-acting beta-agonist, like albuterol, must be at hand, along with resuscitation equipment, and the FEV1 must be back to baseline before the client leaves.

An epinephrine auto-injector is the tempting choice, since a strong reaction is expected, but the reaction is bronchospasm, not an allergy, and albuterol reverses it. An incentive spirometer and a sputum cup aren't part of the test's safety plan.

Takeaway: Bronchoprovocation tests provoke bronchospasm on purpose: albuterol ready, and FEV1 back to baseline before the client leaves.

questions.stem: For each condition, specify whether it is an obstructive or a restrictive lung disease.
rows: Asthma
Emphysema
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Chronic bronchitis
Sarcoidosis
Pneumoconiosis (black lung)
questions.rationale:
Obstructive diseases make it hard to get air out: asthma, and the two parts of COPD, emphysema and chronic bronchitis. Restrictive diseases keep the lungs from expanding: idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, pneumoconiosis (dust diseases like black lung), and sarcoidosis.

The trap is calling every chronic, worsening disease obstructive; the question is whether the trouble is emptying the lungs or filling them.

Takeaway: Obstructive: asthma, emphysema, chronic bronchitis. Restrictive: pulmonary fibrosis, pneumoconiosis, sarcoidosis.

questions.stem: A client has smoked {cig} cigarettes a day for {years} years. How many pack-years is this?
questions.rationale:
A pack is 20 cigarettes, so {cig} cigarettes a day is {=cig / 20} pack(s) a day. Pack-years = packs a day × years smoked = {=cig / 20} × {years} = {answer}.

The usual mistake is multiplying the cigarettes by the years ({=cig * years}), which leaves out turning cigarettes into packs.

Takeaway: Pack-years = (cigarettes a day ÷ 20) × years.

questions.stem: A client reports new wheezing and chest tightness. Which medications in the client's history should the nurse report as possible causes?
options: Propranolol, a beta blocker
Lisinopril, an ACE inhibitor
Ibuprofen, an NSAID
Amiodarone, an antiarrhythmic
Acetaminophen, for headaches
An estrogen-containing birth control pill
questions.rationale:
Wheezing and tightness mean narrowed airways. Beta blockers and NSAIDs can cause bronchoconstriction, so both are worth reporting.

Lisinopril is the tempting one, since ACE inhibitors are known for respiratory side effects, but theirs is a dry cough, not wheezing. Amiodarone can cause lung disease (interstitial lung disease, pleural effusion) over time, estrogen raises the risk of a pulmonary embolism, and acetaminophen doesn't affect the airways.

Takeaway: Wheezing: beta blockers and NSAIDs. Dry cough: ACE inhibitors. Clots: estrogen. Lung scarring: amiodarone and methotrexate.

questions.stem: A client who worked in a shipyard for 30 years has had worsening shortness of breath for a year. Given this occupational history, which condition should the nurse consider?
options: Coal workers' pneumoconiosis (black lung)
Byssinosis, from cotton and other fabric dust
Farmer's lung, an allergic reaction to moldy hay
Asbestosis, from asbestos fibers
questions.rationale:
Shipyard and construction work often meant exposure to asbestos, and asbestosis, a pneumoconiosis (dust disease of the lung), causes slowly worsening shortness of breath years later.

Black lung is the tempting choice, since it's the best-known pneumoconiosis, but it comes from coal mining. Byssinosis comes from fabric factories, and farmer's lung (extrinsic alveolitis) from farm dusts.

Takeaway: Ask about occupation: coal mining (black lung), shipyards and construction (asbestosis), fabric work (byssinosis), farming (extrinsic alveolitis).

questions.stem: A client has sudden shortness of breath and chest pain. Which finding in the client's history should the nurse report as raising the risk of a pulmonary embolism?
options: Has hay fever each spring
Takes an estrogen-containing birth control pill
Had whooping cough as a child
Takes lisinopril for high blood pressure
questions.rationale:
Medicines that contain estrogen raise the risk of blood clots, and so of a pulmonary embolism, along with recent travel, immobility, surgery, cancer, and pregnancy.

Lisinopril is the tempting choice, since it's a medication with respiratory side effects, but its side effect is a dry cough, not clots. Hay fever and childhood whooping cough belong in the respiratory history but don't point to an embolism.

Takeaway: Clot risks in a respiratory history: estrogen, travel, immobility, surgery, cancer, pregnancy.

questions.stem: A client says, “I've been coughing up streaks of blood for two days.” Which part of the medication history should the nurse ask about first?
options: Whether the client uses an inhaled corticosteroid
Whether the client takes an ACE inhibitor for blood pressure
Whether the client takes warfarin, or aspirin
Whether the client recently finished a course of antibiotics
questions.rationale:
Coughing up blood (hemoptysis) can be made worse, or even caused, by medicines that affect clotting: anticoagulants like warfarin, and aspirin.

An ACE inhibitor is the tempting choice, since the client is coughing, but ACE inhibitors cause a dry cough, not bleeding. Inhaled corticosteroids and recent antibiotics belong in the history but don't explain the blood.

Takeaway: Hemoptysis: ask about anticoagulants and aspirin.

questions.stem: For each set of findings over one area of the chest, specify the condition it most likely shows.
rows: Dull percussion, increased tactile fremitus, and crackles
Hyperresonant percussion, decreased tactile fremitus, and absent breath sounds
Dull percussion, decreased tactile fremitus, and decreased breath sounds
Bronchial breath sounds and egophony where vesicular sounds are expected
questions.rationale:
Pneumonia fills the alveoli, so the lung is denser: dull percussion, increased fremitus, crackles, and bronchial breath sounds with egophony. A pneumothorax puts air in the pleural space: hyperresonance, decreased fremitus, and absent or decreased breath sounds. A pleural effusion puts fluid there: dullness with decreased fremitus and breath sounds.

The effusion row is the trap: it's dull like pneumonia, but fluid outside the lung damps the vibrations instead of carrying them.

Takeaway: Dull + fremitus up = consolidation. Dull + fremitus down = fluid. Hyperresonant + fremitus down = air.

questions.stem: A nurse places both hands on a client's back to assess tactile fremitus. Which instruction should the nurse give the client?
options: “Breathe in and out through your mouth, a little deeper than normal.”
“Take a deep breath, and hold it until I tell you to let it out.”
“Cough each time I move my hands to a new spot.”
“Say ‘ninety-nine’ each time I move my hands.”
questions.rationale:
Tactile fremitus is the vibration of the voice felt through the chest wall, so the client speaks (“99”) while the nurse's hands move from side to side and top to bottom.

Breathing through the mouth is the tempting choice, since it's the instruction for auscultation, but fremitus needs the voice. Holding a breath or coughing makes no voice vibration to feel.

Takeaway: Tactile fremitus: hands on the chest, client says “99.”

questions.stem: Over a client's right lower lobe, the nurse hears brief, popping, non-musical sounds during inspiration. How should the nurse document them?
options: Crackles
Rhonchi
Wheezes
Pleural friction rub
questions.rationale:
Brief, popping, discontinuous, non-musical sounds are crackles, heard in pneumonia, heart failure, and COPD.

Rhonchi are the tempting choice, since both come from secretions, but rhonchi are continuous, low-pitched, musical sounds. Wheezes are continuous and high-pitched, and a friction rub is a grating sound from inflamed pleura.

Takeaway: Crackles pop (discontinuous). Rhonchi and wheezes are continuous: rhonchi low, wheezes high.

questions.stem: A nurse auscultates the lungs of four clients. Which client's finding should the nurse report first?
options: Crackles at both lung bases in a client with heart failure, unchanged from yesterday
Scattered rhonchi that clear after a client coughs
A loud, high-pitched sound on each breath in, in a client whose lips are swelling
Expiratory wheezes in a client with asthma who used a rescue inhaler 5 minutes ago
questions.rationale:
A loud, high-pitched sound on breathing in is stridor, from a narrowing upper airway, and with swelling lips it points to an allergic reaction that can close the airway. Airway comes first.

The wheezes are the tempting choice, since asthma can be serious, but the client just used a rescue inhaler, which takes a few minutes to work; that's a reassessment, not the first call. Unchanged crackles and rhonchi that clear with coughing are stable findings.

Takeaway: Stridor is an airway emergency. Airway, breathing, circulation decide who comes first.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old client with a 50 pack-year smoking history has a chest whose front-to-back diameter about equals its side-to-side diameter. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
options: It's a normal finding, as it is in young children
It shows a depressed sternum (pectus excavatum)
It suggests hyperinflation of the lungs, as in COPD
It points to a sideways curve of the spine (scoliosis)
questions.rationale:
A barrel chest, with a front-to-back diameter about equal to the side-to-side diameter, suggests hyperinflation in an adult: trapped air, as in COPD, which fits a 50 pack-year history.

“Normal, as in young children” is the tempting choice, since a barrel chest is normal in children, but in an adult it's a finding to note. Pectus excavatum is a sunken sternum, and scoliosis is a sideways curve of the spine.

Takeaway: Barrel chest: normal in children; in adults, think air trapping (COPD).

questions.stem: Over most of a healthy adult's lung fields, the nurse hears soft, low-pitched breath sounds. How should the nurse document them?
options: Diminished breath sounds, which need follow-up
Vesicular breath sounds, which are normal
Bronchial breath sounds, which are normal there
Wheezes, which need follow-up
questions.rationale:
Soft, low-pitched sounds over most of the lung fields are vesicular breath sounds, the normal sound of air moving through the smaller airways.

Diminished is the tempting choice, since the sounds are soft, but soft is normal over the lung fields. Bronchial sounds are loud and high-pitched (normal only over the trachea), and wheezes are musical.

Takeaway: Vesicular = normal over the lung fields. Bronchial sounds there are abnormal (consolidation).

questions.stem: Place the steps of the chest and lung exam in the order the nurse performs them.
questions.rationale:
The chest is examined by inspection (breathing pattern, accessory muscles, position, chest shape), palpation (masses, tactile fremitus), percussion (resonance or dullness), then auscultation (breath sounds).

The trap is the abdominal exam's order, which moves auscultation up to second; for the chest, it stays last.

Takeaway: Chest: inspect, palpate, percuss, auscultate.

questions.stem: A client's spirometry shows a low FEV1/FVC ratio. After the client inhales albuterol, the FEV1 improves markedly. Which condition does this pattern suggest?
options: Asthma
Emphysema
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
A pneumothorax
questions.rationale:
A low FEV1/FVC ratio means obstruction, and an obstruction that reverses with a beta-agonist like albuterol is the mark of asthma.

Emphysema is the tempting choice, since it's obstructive too, but its damage (lost alveolar elasticity) doesn't reverse with a bronchodilator. Pulmonary fibrosis is restrictive, with a normal or high ratio.

Takeaway: Obstruction that reverses with albuterol: asthma. Obstruction that doesn't: COPD.

questions.stem: A client who recently arrived from a country where tuberculosis is common has had a cough for 2 months, night sweats, weight loss, and blood-streaked sputum. What should the nurse do first?
options: Collect a sputum specimen for testing
Ask about family members and close contacts who have been sick
Place a mask on the client, and arrange an airborne isolation room
Teach the client to cover the mouth and nose when coughing
questions.rationale:
Cough, night sweats, weight loss, and hemoptysis in a client from a high-risk area point to active tuberculosis, which spreads through the air. Before anything else, the nurse protects others: a mask on the client, and an airborne isolation room (staff wear fitted N95 respirators).

Collecting a sputum specimen is the tempting choice, since it confirms the diagnosis, but it comes after the client is isolated. Asking about contacts and teaching cough etiquette matter too, but don't protect people right now.

Takeaway: Suspected TB: isolate first (airborne precautions), then test.

questions.stem: A tall, thin 22-year-old suddenly has sharp right-sided chest pain and shortness of breath. Which findings should the nurse expect on the right side of the chest?
options: Dull percussion, and bronchial breath sounds
Dull percussion, with a grating pleural friction rub
Resonant percussion, with expiratory wheezes
Hyperresonant percussion, and absent or decreased breath sounds
questions.rationale:
Sudden sharp chest pain and dyspnea in a tall, thin young adult suggest a spontaneous pneumothorax: air in the pleural space. Air is hyperresonant, and it keeps sound from reaching the chest wall, so breath sounds are decreased or absent, and so is fremitus.

Dull percussion with bronchial breath sounds is the tempting choice, since it's a classic set of findings, but it means denser lung (consolidation), the opposite of air. A friction rub comes from inflamed pleura, and wheezes from narrowed airways.

Takeaway: Air in the chest: hyperresonance, with decreased breath sounds and fremitus.

questions.stem: A client has sharp chest pain that gets worse with each deep breath. Over the painful area, the nurse hears a grating sound during both inspiration and expiration. Which condition do these findings suggest?
options: A pneumothorax
Pleurisy
Pneumonia
An asthma attack
questions.rationale:
Pleurisy (inflamed pleura) causes sharp pain that worsens with breathing in, and the inflamed layers rub together, making a grating pleural friction rub in both phases of breathing.

A pneumothorax is the tempting choice, since it also causes sudden, sharp pleuritic pain, but air separates the pleural layers, so breath sounds are decreased, with no rub. Pneumonia brings crackles, and asthma brings wheezes.

Takeaway: Pleural friction rub: inflamed pleura rubbing together (pleurisy).

questions.stem: A client with influenza is recovering at home. Which findings should the nurse teach the client's family to report right away, as signs that the illness is becoming severe?
options: Shortness of breath
Aching muscles in the back and legs
A fast heart rate
Dizziness or fainting on standing, from low blood pressure
A runny nose, sneezing, and a sore throat
A headache behind the eyes, with sensitivity to light
questions.rationale:
Severe influenza can bring shortness of breath, a fast heart rate, and low blood pressure, and it can get there within about 48 hours, so the family reports these right away.

A headache behind the eyes is the tempting one, since it sounds worrying, but a frontal or behind-the-eyes headache is a common part of ordinary influenza, along with muscle aches, a runny nose, and a sore throat.

Takeaway: Influenza turning severe: shortness of breath, a fast heart rate, low blood pressure.

questions.stem: A nurse is about to assess a hospitalized client who has influenza. Which personal protective equipment should the nurse wear, beyond standard precautions?
options: A face mask, for droplet precautions
A fitted N95 respirator, for airborne precautions
A gown and gloves, for contact precautions
Nothing more, since standard precautions cover influenza
questions.rationale:
Influenza spreads mainly by droplets from coughs and sneezes, so the nurse follows droplet precautions: a face mask when entering the room, on top of standard precautions like hand hygiene.

A fitted N95 respirator is the tempting choice, since it gives the most protection, but that's for diseases spread through the air over longer distances, like tuberculosis. Contact precautions are for infections spread by touch.

Takeaway: Influenza: droplet precautions (face mask). Tuberculosis: airborne precautions (N95 respirator).

questions.stem: A 70-year-old client asks, “Why do I need a flu shot every year?” Which response should the nurse give?
options: “Flu viruses change, so each season's vaccine is updated, and vaccinated people tend to have milder illness.”
“Your immunity from last year's shot has worn off, and the same vaccine is given each year to renew it.”
“The vaccine treats the flu if you catch it, so you need it before each flu season.”
“Adults over 65 need it yearly, while younger adults need it once in 5 years.”
questions.rationale:
Many strains of influenza virus circulate, and they change, so each season's vaccine is updated to match. People who get the seasonal vaccine tend to have milder symptoms and fewer complications.

“The same vaccine renews your immunity” is the tempting choice, since protection does wane, but the vaccine itself changes each year. It prevents illness rather than treating it, and yearly vaccination is advised for adults of every age.

Takeaway: Flu vaccine: every year, because the viruses change; vaccinated people have milder illness.

questions.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the Day 4 note that point to pneumonia in the right lower lobe.
questions.passage: Resident is [[newly confused about the day and place]], and is [[coughing up thick, rust-colored sputum]]. Reports a [[sharp pain in the right lower chest when breathing in]]. [[Ate 25% of breakfast]]. [[Respirations labored]]. Right lower posterior chest: [[dull to percussion]], [[increased tactile fremitus]], [[bronchial breath sounds and crackles]]. Left lung: [[vesicular breath sounds]]. [[Lips pink]].
questions.rationale:
Pneumonia fills the alveoli of a lobe (consolidation). Over the right lower lobe, that shows as dull percussion, increased tactile fremitus, and bronchial breath sounds with crackles, and the rust-colored sputum and pain on breathing in on that side fit a bacterial pneumonia that involves the pleura.

New confusion and labored breathing are the tempting ones: they're serious and need reporting, but they don't point to the right lower lobe. The left lung's vesicular sounds are normal, and pink lips show no cyanosis.

Takeaway: Consolidation over a lobe: dull, fremitus up, bronchial sounds and crackles, plus purulent or rust-colored sputum.

questions.stem: For each finding, specify whether it fits influenza alone or a new pneumonia in the right lower lobe.
columns: New pneumonia in the right lower lobe
rows: Muscle aches and a sore throat on Day 1
Dull percussion over the right lower lobe on Day 4
Dry cough on Day 1
Bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lobe on Day 4
Thick, rust-colored sputum on Day 4
questions.rationale:
Day 1's muscle aches, sore throat, and dry cough are typical of influenza itself. Day 4's dullness and bronchial breath sounds over one lobe, with rust-colored sputum, show a consolidation: pneumonia, a common complication of influenza in older adults.

The cough is the trap: both illnesses cause one, but influenza's is dry, while a bacterial pneumonia brings up purulent or rust-colored sputum.

Takeaway: Influenza that gets worse after a few days, with new lobar findings, suggests a pneumonia on top of it.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the resident's Day 4 findings and vital signs.

options: Pneumothorax
Pneumonia
Pleural effusion
An asthma attack
Report the Day 4 findings to the provider
Lay the resident flat to rest
Keep the resident on droplet precautions
Encourage fluids, and recheck in the afternoon
Stop the droplet precautions, since the problem is now pneumonia
Oxygen saturation
Bowel sounds in each quadrant
Respiratory rate and effort
Blood glucose before meals
Pupil size and reaction to light

questions.rationale:
Dullness, increased fremitus, bronchial sounds, crackles, rust-colored sputum, and a new fever spike point to pneumonia. The nurse reports it now (the saturation is 88% and the blood pressure is falling) and keeps droplet precautions, since the resident still has influenza. The nurse watches the oxygen saturation and the respiratory rate and effort.

Encouraging fluids and rechecking later is the tempting action, since fluids help, but waiting hours with these findings delays treatment. Lying flat makes breathing harder, and pneumonia doesn't end the influenza precautions. A pneumothorax or effusion would make breath sounds decrease, not turn bronchial.

Takeaway: Lobar consolidation with worsening vital signs: report now, keep the precautions, and watch the oxygenation closely.

questions.stem: The resident's daughter arrives on Day 4 and wants to sit at the bedside. Which instruction should the nurse give her?
options: “Wear a fitted N95 respirator, since influenza can spread through the air across the room.”
“Wear a gown and gloves, and sit at least 3 feet from the bed instead of wearing a mask.”
“Wear a face mask in the room, and clean your hands when you leave.”
“You won't need any precautions, since you had a flu shot this year.”
questions.rationale:
The resident is on droplet precautions: visitors wear a face mask in the room, and everyone cleans their hands on the way out.

“You had a flu shot” is the tempting choice, since vaccination does lower her risk, but it doesn't make her immune, and the precautions also keep her from carrying the virus to others. An N95 respirator is for airborne diseases, and distance plus a gown doesn't replace the mask.

Takeaway: Droplet precautions apply to visitors too: a face mask in the room, and hand hygiene.

questions.stem: Which Day 4 findings should the nurse report as signs that the resident's oxygenation is getting worse?
options: Oxygen saturation of 88% on room air
New confusion about the day and place
Respiratory rate of 30/min, labored
Temperature of 39.3 °C (102.7 °F), up from 38.6 °C
Ate 25% of breakfast that morning
Lips pink, with no bluish color
questions.rationale:
A saturation of 88% (down from 95%), new confusion (the brain is sensitive to low oxygen, especially in older adults), and a fast, labored respiratory rate all show worsening oxygenation.

The fever is the tempting one, since it rose too, but it shows infection, not oxygenation. A poor appetite is common in illness, and pink lips mean no cyanosis yet, which shouldn't reassure the nurse given the other findings.

Takeaway: Signs of worsening oxygenation: a falling SpO₂, new confusion, a rising respiratory rate and effort.
